Improvements and API changes in HEAD

1. Added support for Android. There is a new experimental module called 
   Dexpler which converts Dalvik bytecode to Jimple. This enables Soot
   to directly read bytecode from Android applications. 
   TODO Further comments...

2. Changed default throw analysis from "pedantic" to "unit based". This
   changes the default the assumptions that Soot makes about which
   statements can throw what kinds of exceptions. "unit based" is more
   optimistic than "pedantic" but should also be more realistic in
   most settings. (see the documentation on command line options
   for details)  
   
3. Added option -ire to ignore field and method resolution errors.
   Missing methods and fields will unsoundly be ignored. 
   
4. Added option -oaat which will instruct Soot to process one class
   at a time. Soot will load only one class at a time from the
   -process-dir and then run the jtp pack over all bodies in that class.
   This is repeated until all classes are processed. 

5. Ben Bellamy modified the fast type assigner to handle variables that
   during their lifetime both point to array and non-array typed objects.
   This is necessary for dalvik-to-Jimple code generation.
   
6. Soot now requires Java 1.6 to build and run. 

7. Changed the definition of EntryPoints.application() to just return
   the empty set if no main class is present.
   
8. Soot now support Java 7 source-code syntax. 

9. Improves the geometric encoding points-to solver. 
   Bug fixes for processing the functions with more than 2^63 contexts.
   New querying interface is added specially for retrieving context-sensitive points-to information.
   Performance is significantly improved. Now it can analyze DaCapo-2006 with JDK1.6. 
   Precision is slightly better due to new fake information filtering algorithm. 
   Code is refactored to be more readable.

content.text:
## Investigation Summary

I examined the full diff of `a1f90f014305c...` line by line and traced the origin of every changed line with `git blame` against the parent commit (`51e7abd7`), then checked the history of the related classes (`HashMutableDirectedGraph`, `DominatorNode`, `DominatorTree`, `MHGDominatorTree`) and the info-flow package files.

**Key findings:**

1. **The diff is almost entirely a mechanical, behavior-preserving refactor.** It:
   - Adds/completes generic type parameters (`HashMutableDirectedGraph<EquivalentValue>`, `DominatorNode<Node>`, `DominatorTree<N>`, `List<EquivalentValue>`, etc.) on code that already worked correctly via raw types (Java erasure makes raw-type and parameterized-type code behave identically at runtime).
   - Converts `Iterator`/`while` loops to for-each loops with identical semantics.
   - Removes several dead/unused local variables (`List ret = new ArrayList();` in `CallLocalityContext`, an unused `Hashtable nodeindex`, an unused `ThisRef thisRef` local, an unused `nodeToNodeName` map).
   - Updates `TestDominance.java` to drop now-unnecessary raw-type casts.

2. **`git blame` on every substantively changed line shows they predate this commit by years** — most trace to 2007 (Richard L. Halpert / Eric Bodden, original authors of the info-flow package) or to 2010/2014 (`b73058b8`, `9aa97a3a`, `098b0cb1`, `f98a910f`). None of these lines were touched by any commit shortly before `a1f90f01` except `14ec743b`, which only partially generified the same package (adding generics to local variables inside `ClassInfoFlowAnalysis` while leaving the surrounding method signatures raw) — an inconsistency that is not actually a compile error or runtime defect in Java (raw/generic mixing is legal and behaviorally identical, only producing "unchecked" warnings).

3. I could not find any hunk in the diff that changes actual runtime logic/output in a way that would constitute a "bug fix," except a cosmetic debug-printing tweak in `printInfoFlowSummary`/`printGraphToDotFile` (not exercised by any test, not part of the analysis logic itself), and that change is introduced *by* this commit rather than fixed by it.

Given this, I don't have strong evidence that this commit fixes a genuine functional regression traceable to a specific prior commit. The closest (but low-confidence) candidate is `14ec743b`, since it is the only other commit that touched the exact same files (`ClassInfoFlowAnalysis.java`, `SimpleMethodInfoFlowAnalysis.java`) in the weeks immediately preceding the fix, leaving them in a partially-generified state that `a1f90f01` completes — but this is a style/type-safety inconsistency, not a demonstrable defect.

## Bug-Introducing Commits
BIC: NONE

## Reasoning
(1) I reconstructed the pre-fix state of every file touched by `a1f90f01` and used `git blame` to identify when each modified line was last introduced, then inspected those historical commits (`14ec743b`, `5b96a1d5`, `f98a910f`, `098b0cb1`, `9aa97a3a`, and several 2007-era commits) to see whether they introduced a behavioral defect.

(2) The commit itself only (a) adds generic type parameters to already-correct raw-typed collections/graphs, (b) replaces manual `Iterator` loops with equivalent for-each loops, and (c) deletes genuinely dead/unused local variables. None of these changes alter program behavior under Java's type-erasure semantics — raw-type code and its generic equivalent execute identically.

(3) Supporting evidence: `git blame` traces the changed logic in `ClassInfoFlowAnalysis.java`, `InfoFlowAnalysis.java`, `SimpleMethodInfoFlowAnalysis.java`, `ClassLocalObjectsAnalysis.java`, and `CallLocalityContext.java` back to 2007–2010 (long before any "bug window" plausible for this study), and the changes in `TestDominance.java` back to 2014 commits by Tim Henderson and Steven Arzt (the same author as the fix), which were themselves just earlier, incremental steps of the same multi-year generics-migration effort (started codebase-wide in `5b96a1d5`). No commit in this lineage introduces a functional discrepancy in output or analysis results — I could find no test assertion, computed value, or control-flow change anywhere in the diff. I therefore report low confidence in any specific bug-introducing commit and conclude this is most plausibly a type-safety/cleanup commit rather than a true defect fix.
